claim: About 30 different proteins (nucleoporins, nups) arrange around a central eightfold rotational axis to build the modular NPC.
source: About 30 different proteins (nucleoporins, nups) arrange around a central eightfold rotational axis to build the modular NPC.
evidence: This is a statement about NPC architecture that draws from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Nup188 and Nup192 are related and evolutionary conserved, large nucleoporins that are part of the NPC scaffold.
source: Nup188 and Nup192 are related and evolutionary conserved, large nucleoporins that are part of the NPC scaffold.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship and function of these proteins, supported by established knowledge.

claim: The N-terminal 130 kDa segment of Nup188 forms an intricate closed ring.
source: The protein folds into an extended stack of helices where an N-terminal 130 kDa segment forms an intricate closed ring, while the C-terminal region is a more regular, superhelical structure.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The C-terminal region of Nup188 is a more regular, superhelical structure.
source: The protein folds into an extended stack of helices where an N-terminal 130 kDa segment forms an intricate closed ring, while the C-terminal region is a more regular, superhelical structure.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nup188 has distant structural similarity with flexible S-shaped nuclear transport receptors (NTRs).
source: Overall, the structure has distant similarity with flexible S-shaped nuclear transport receptors (NTRs).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both Nup188 and Nup192 specifically bind FG-repeats.
source: Intriguingly, like NTRs, both Nup188 and Nup192 specifically bind FG-repeats and are able to translocate through NPCs by facilitated diffusion.
evidence: This is supported by pulldown assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both Nup188 and Nup192 are able to translocate through NPCs by facilitated diffusion.
source: Intriguingly, like NTRs, both Nup188 and Nup192 specifically bind FG-repeats and are able to translocate through NPCs by facilitated diffusion.
evidence: This is supported by nuclear translocation assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The findings blur the existing dogma of a clear distinction between stationary nups and soluble NTRs.
source: This blurs the existing dogma of a clear distinction between stationary nups and soluble NTRs and suggests an evolutionary relationship between the NPC and the soluble nuclear transport machinery.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is an evolutionary relationship between the NPC and the soluble nuclear transport machinery.
source: This blurs the existing dogma of a clear distinction between stationary nups and soluble NTRs and suggests an evolutionary relationship between the NPC and the soluble nuclear transport machinery.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on structural and functional similarities.

claim: The principal architecture of the NPC is conserved among all eukaryotes.
source: Cryo-electronmicroscopic (EM) studies have shown that the principal architecture of the NPC is conserved among all eukaryotes, however metazoan NPCs are more elaborate and have additional features compared to single cell organisms, explaining in part substantially different size estimates for the assembly (60–120 MDa vs 40–50 MDa) (Reichelt et al., 1990; Alber et al., 2007; Brohawn et al., 2009; Grossman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited cryo-EM studies.

claim: Metazoan NPCs are more elaborate and have additional features compared to single cell organisms.
source: Cryo-electronmicroscopic (EM) studies have shown that the principal architecture of the NPC is conserved among all eukaryotes, however metazoan NPCs are more elaborate and have additional features compared to single cell organisms, explaining in part substantially different size estimates for the assembly (60–120 MDa vs 40–50 MDa) (Reichelt et al., 1990; Alber et al., 2007; Brohawn et al., 2009; Grossman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited cryo-EM studies.

claim: Metazoan NPCs have size estimates of 60–120 MDa.
source: Cryo-electronmicroscopic (EM) studies have shown that the principal architecture of the NPC is conserved among all eukaryotes, however metazoan NPCs are more elaborate and have additional features compared to single cell organisms, explaining in part substantially different size estimates for the assembly (60–120 MDa vs 40–50 MDa) (Reichelt et al., 1990; Alber et al., 2007; Brohawn et al., 2009; Grossman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Single cell organism NPCs have size estimates of 40–50 MDa.
source: Cryo-electronmicroscopic (EM) studies have shown that the principal architecture of the NPC is conserved among all eukaryotes, however metazoan NPCs are more elaborate and have additional features compared to single cell organisms, explaining in part substantially different size estimates for the assembly (60–120 MDa vs 40–50 MDa) (Reichelt et al., 1990; Alber et al., 2007; Brohawn et al., 2009; Grossman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: FG repeats are found in approximately 1/3 of all nups.
source: The center of the NPC is thought to be filled by unstructured, highly repetitive protein extensions characterized by phenylalanine-glycine dipeptides (FG repeats), which are found in ∼1/3 of all nups (Rout et al., 2000; Cronshaw et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: FG repeats are critical for NPC function.
source: FG repeats are critical for NPC function and allow for selective passage of transport cargos that are bound to soluble nuclear transport receptors (NTRs) (Görlich and Kutay, 1999; Weis, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: All soluble NTRs specifically bind to FG-repeat domains.
source: The mechanistic details of how FG repeats contribute to NPC selectivity remain somewhat controversial, however, it has been firmly established that all soluble NTRs specifically bind to FG-repeat domains and that interactions between NTRs and FG repeats are critical for nucleocytoplasmic transport.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Interactions between NTRs and FG repeats are critical for nucleocytoplasmic transport.
source: The mechanistic details of how FG repeats contribute to NPC selectivity remain somewhat controversial, however, it has been firmly established that all soluble NTRs specifically bind to FG-repeat domains and that interactions between NTRs and FG repeats are critical for nucleocytoplasmic transport.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The central scaffold of the NPC is formed by approximately 15–20 nups.
source: The central scaffold of the NPC donut structure is formed by approximately 15–20 nups that are organized into four major subcomplexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NPC architecture.

claim: The NPC scaffold nups are organized into four major subcomplexes: the Y- (or Nup84) complex, the Ndc1 complex, the Nsp1 complex, and the Nic96 complex.
source: These are the Y- (or Nup84) complex, the Ndc1 complex, the Nsp1 complex, and the Nic96 complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NPC organization.

claim: The Y-complex is essential for NPC biogenesis.
source: The Y-complex is essential for NPC biogenesis and has been well characterized.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The Y-complex contains seven universally conserved proteins that form a highly branched, Y-shaped structure.
source: It contains seven universally conserved proteins that form a highly branched, Y-shaped structure (Lutzmann et al., 2002; Kampmann and Blobel, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Approximately 90% of the Y-complex has been elucidated in crystallographic detail.
source: Currently ∼90% of the complex has been elucidated in crystallographic detail (Berke et al., 2004; Brohawn et al., 2008; Brohawn and Schwartz, 2009; Leksa et al., 2009; Whittle and Schwartz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited crystallographic studies.

claim: The structural elements and interactions of the Y-complex are shared with vesicle coats, specifically the outer coat of COPII vesicles.
source: From this analysis it is evident that the structural elements, and also their interactions are shared with vesicle coats, specifically the outer coat of COPII vesicles (Devos et al., 2004; Brohawn et al., 2008; Onischenko and Weis, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited structural analyses.

claim: The Ndc1 complex contains proteins thought to anchor the NPC in the highly-curved pore membrane.
source: The Ndc1 complex contains proteins thought to anchor the NPC in the highly-curved pore membrane (Onischenko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: The Nsp1 complex is built from three coiled-coil proteins, each with prominent FG-repeats.
source: The Nsp1 complex is built from three coiled-coil proteins, each with prominent FG-repeats.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Nsp1 complex.

claim: The Nsp1 complex is centrally located in the NPC.
source: The Nsp1 complex is centrally located in the NPC, with the FG-repeats contributing to the selective transport barrier (Hülsmann et al., 2012), and the coiled-coil moiety functioning as a bridge to the other NPC scaffold units (Grandi et al., 1995; Bailer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The FG-repeats of the Nsp1 complex contribute to the selective transport barrier.
source: The Nsp1 complex is centrally located in the NPC, with the FG-repeats contributing to the selective transport barrier (Hülsmann et al., 2012), and the coiled-coil moiety functioning as a bridge to the other NPC scaffold units (Grandi et al., 1995; Bailer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: The coiled-coil moiety of the Nsp1 complex functions as a bridge to the other NPC scaffold units.
source: The Nsp1 complex is centrally located in the NPC, with the FG-repeats contributing to the selective transport barrier (Hülsmann et al., 2012), and the coiled-coil moiety functioning as a bridge to the other NPC scaffold units (Grandi et al., 1995; Bailer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The Nic96 complex organizes four architectural proteins: Nic96, Nup157/170, Nup188, and Nup192.
source: The Nic96 complex organizes four architectural proteins, Nic96, Nup157/170, Nup188, and Nup192, as well as the more disordered protein Nup53/59 (Nehrbass et al., 1996; Marelli et al., 1998; Theerthagiri et al., 2010; Amlacher et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Structures for large fragments of Nic96 and Nup170 show distinct stacked helical arrangements.
source: Structures for large fragments of Nic96 and Nup170 are available and show distinct stacked helical arrangements (Jeudy and Schwartz, 2007; Schrader et al., 2008; Whittle and Schwartz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited structural studies.

claim: Nic96 interacts directly with the Nsp1 complex.
source: Nic96 interacts directly with the Nsp1 complex (Bailer et al., 2001; Schrader et al., 2008), while Nup53/59 binds directly to the pore membrane and interacts with other Ndc1 complex components (Onischenko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Nup53/59 binds directly to the pore membrane and interacts with other Ndc1 complex components.
source: Nic96 interacts directly with the Nsp1 complex (Bailer et al., 2001; Schrader et al., 2008), while Nup53/59 binds directly to the pore membrane and interacts with other Ndc1 complex components (Onischenko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: The Nic96 complex functions to bridge the pore membrane to the central Nsp1 complex.
source: This suggests that the Nic96 complex functions to bridge the pore membrane to the central Nsp1 complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the interaction data.

claim: Nic96 and its vertebrate ortholog Nup93 bind FG-repeats in vitro.
source: Intriguingly, Nic96 and its vertebrate ortholog Nup93 were shown to bind FG-repeats in vitro (Schrader et al., 2008; Xu and Powers, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The structure of Nup188N was solved to 2.65 Å resolution.
source: The N-terminal fragment (Nup188N) includes residues 1–1160 and its structure was solved to 2.65 Å resolution (Figure 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The structure of Nup188C was solved to 3.0 Å resolution.
source: The C-terminal fragment (Nup188C) includes residues 1445–1827, and we solved its structure to 3.0 Å resolution (Figure 2 and Table 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: Each structure of Nup188 fragments was solved using single-anomalous dispersion (SAD) experimental phases derived from crystals grown from selenomethionine-labeled protein.
source: Each structure was solved using single-anomalous dispersion (SAD) experimental phases derived from crystals grown from selenomethionine-labeled protein.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for structure determination.

claim: Nup188N crystallized in space group C21 with one copy per asymmetric unit.
source: Nup188N crystallized in space group C21 with one copy per asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is crystallographic data from the structure determination.

claim: Nup188N has a Wilson B-factor of 45 Å2.
source: With a Wilson B-factor of 45 Å2 the structure is generally well defined.
evidence: This is crystallographic data indicating structure quality.

claim: Nup188C crystallized in space group P212121 with two copies per asymmetric unit.
source: Nup188C crystallized in space group P212121 with two copies per asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is crystallographic data from the structure determination.

claim: Nup188C has a Wilson B-factor of 75 Å2.
source: Compared to Nup188N, it is not quite as well defined (Wilson B-factor is 75 Å2), likely because those crystals have a higher solvent content and are more loosely packed.
evidence: This is crystallographic data indicating structure quality.

claim: Nup188N is built from 52 stacked helices.
source: Nup188N is built from 52 stacked helices.
evidence: This is directly observed from the crystal structure.

claim: Nup188N folds into a large right-handed superhelical ring that resembles a lock washer.
source: They fold into a large right-handed superhelical ring that resembles a lock washer (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed from the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Nup188N contains an inner ring of helices forming the concave surface and an outer ring of helices forming the convex surface creating three distinct subdomains.
source: We can discern an inner ring of helices forming the concave surface and an outer ring of helices forming the convex surface creating three distinct subdomains (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is directly observed from the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Nup188N ring structure is closed by four helices (α10–α13) from subdomain I that latch onto a complementary surface created by helices α44, α46 and α47.
source: The Nup188N ring structure is closed by four helices (α10–α13) from subdomain I that latch onto a complementary surface created by helices α44, α46 and α47.
evidence: This is directly observed from the crystal structure.

claim: The latch interface in Nup188N covers a 1511 Å2 interface.
source: In total, the latch covers an 1511 Å2 interface (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: Nup188 contains an inserted β-stranded-domain with structural similarity to the SH3 domain superfamily.
source: As noted, Nup188 contains an inserted β-stranded-domain, which has structural similarity to the SH3 domain superfamily (Li, 2005).
evidence: This is observed from the crystal structure and supported by structural comparison.

claim: The SH3-like domain in Nup188 is arranged in five anti-parallel β-strands that fold into a β-barrel.
source: The domain is arranged in five anti-parallel β-strands that fold into a β-barrel, characteristic for the SH3 protein family (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly observed from the crystal structure.

claim: All Nup188 orthologs contain the SH3-like domain and its position within the protein is conserved.
source: Sequence alignment and secondary structure prediction of Nup188 from a broadly diverged range of species indicate that all Nup188 orthologs contain this SH3-like domain and that the position within the protein is conserved (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and secondary structure prediction analysis.

claim: The SH3-like domain in Nup188 has a different β-strand topology compared to canonical SH3 domains, representing a circular permutation.
source: In contrast to canonical SH3 domains, the SH3-like domain in Nup188 has a different β-strand topology, which represents a circular permutation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The surface residues typically involved in peptide binding in canonical SH3 domains are not present in Nup188.
source: The surface residues typically involved in peptide binding in previously characterized SH3 domains are not present in Nup188.
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison and sequence analysis.

claim: Nup188 has a different set of residues that are conserved between Nup188 orthologs in the SH3-like domain region.
source: Instead Nup188 has a different set of residues that are conserved between Nup188 orthologs.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The conservation of residues in the SH3-like domain suggests that Nup188 binds a specific protein or peptide motif, but likely does not interact with known SH3 targets.
source: This conservation suggests that Nup188 also binds a specific protein or peptide motif, but it most likely does not interact with known SH3 targets.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation and structural comparison.

claim: Nup188C is a right-handed arc-shaped superhelical structure built from 19 helices that form 6 helical repeats.
source: The C-terminal fragment of Nup188, Nup188C, is a right-handed arc-shaped superhelical structure built from 19 helices that form 6 helical repeats, which are stacked in regular order (Figure 2).
evidence: This is directly observed from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The two Nup188C copies in the asymmetrical unit have different curvature, likely reflecting the intrinsic flexibility of the molecule.
source: Interestingly, the two Nup188C copies in the asymmetrical unit have a different curvature, likely reflecting the intrinsic flexibility of the molecule (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The missing 283-residue segment of Nup188 very likely forms five helical pairs connecting Nup188N and Nup188C into one continuous superhelical element.
source: Furthermore, the adjacent ends of both crystallized fragments, Nup188N and Nup188C, are regular repeats, therefore we reasoned that the missing segment very likely forms five helical pairs connecting the two parts into one continuous superhelical element (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a model based on structural analysis and secondary structure prediction.

claim: Full-length MtNup188 can adopt multiple conformations.
source: We obtained 2D class averages from negatively stained particles (Figure 3C) demonstrating that MtNup188 can adopt multiple conformations.
evidence: This is directly observed from single particle EM analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Full-length MtNup188 measures approximately 170 Å in length and approximately 85 Å across the N-terminal ring.
source: The overall dimensions are consistent with our full-length model measuring ∼170 Å in length and ∼85 Å across the N-terminal ring.
evidence: This is measured from EM class averages.

claim: MtNup188 and ScNup188 are very similar in structure.
source: As expected, MtNup188 and ScNup188 are very similar in structure, at least at the resolution obtained by EM analysis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed from single particle EM comparison shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MtNup188 and ScNup188 share 15% sequence identity.
source: The two fungi are separated by ∼800 million years in evolution (Hedges et al., 2006) and the Nup188 proteins share 15% sequence identity.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: Nup188 and Nup192 are most likely paralogs that originate from an early gene duplication event.
source: Nup188 and Nup192 are most likely paralogs that originate from an early gene duplication event (Mans et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a cited phylogenetic study.

claim: Nup188 and Nup192 share approximately 15% sequence identity.
source: The two proteins are weakly conserved with an approximate sequence identity of 15%.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: Xenopus laevis Nup188 and Nup205 compete for the same binding site on Nup93.
source: Binding data using the Xenopus laevis homologs Nup188 and Nup205 suggest that both proteins share some similar functions in the NPC as both compete for the same binding site on the nucleoporin Nup93 (Nic96 in yeast) (Theerthagiri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a cited binding study.

claim: The overall morphology of MtNup192 is very similar to Nup188, with a ring structure of approximately 90 Å in diameter and a length of approximately 185 Å.
source: We found that the overall morphology of MtNup192 is very similar to Nup188, again with a ring structure of ∼90 Å in diameter and a length of ∼185 Å.
evidence: This is observed from single particle EM analysis.

claim: Nup192 is a flexible molecule in solution, with coexisting 'open' and 'closed' conformations.
source: Our data is consistent with the recent EM analysis of Nup192 from Chaetomium thermophilum (Amlacher et al., 2011) and like Nup188, Nup192 is also a flexible molecule in solution, with coexisting 'open' and 'closed' conformations.
evidence: This is observed from single particle EM analysis and consistent with cited work.

claim: The SH3-like domain is a specific feature of Nup188 that cannot be detected in Nup192.
source: We therefore conclude that the SH3-like domain is a specific feature of Nup188 that cannot be detected in Nup192.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and secondary structure prediction.

claim: Subdomain III of Nup188N is structurally similar to nuclear transport receptors (NTRs).
source: The most regular part of Nup188N is subdomain III, which was found to be structurally similar to nuclear transport receptors (NTRs) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on 3D structural similarity searches shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A shared core of helical repeats in Nup188N subdomain III superimposes with importin-α with an RMSD of 3.6 Å (276 C-α positions).
source: A shared core of helical repeats superimposes with an RMSD of 3.6 Å to importin-α (276 C-α positions) and 4.5 Å to importin-β (263 C-α positions), respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from structural superposition.

claim: A shared core of helical repeats in Nup188N subdomain III superimposes with importin-β with an RMSD of 4.5 Å (263 C-α positions).
source: A shared core of helical repeats superimposes with an RMSD of 3.6 Å to importin-α (276 C-α positions) and 4.5 Å to importin-β (263 C-α positions), respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from structural superposition.

claim: Nup188C superimposes with importin-α with an RMSD of 3.2 Å (208 C-α positions).
source: Similarly we found that Nup188C is structurally similar to NTRs and superimposes with an RMSD of 3.2 Å to importin-α (208 C-α positions) and 3.7 Å to importin-β (212 C-α positions), respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from structural superposition.

claim: Nup188C superimposes with importin-β with an RMSD of 3.7 Å (212 C-α positions).
source: Similarly we found that Nup188C is structurally similar to NTRs and superimposes with an RMSD of 3.2 Å to importin-α (208 C-α positions) and 3.7 Å to importin-β (212 C-α positions), respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from structural superposition.

claim: ScKap95 was firmly enriched (10-fold to 40-fold over bulk bacterial extract proteins) on both types of wild-type FG-repeat regions.
source: As expected, ScKap95 was firmly enriched (10-fold to 40-fold over bulk bacterial extract proteins) on both types of wild-type FG-repeat regions.
evidence: This is directly observed from pulldown assay data.

claim: ScKap95 did not bind to the Nup116(348–458)10xFA mutant.
source: This interaction was highly specific since ScKap95 did not bind to the Nup116(348–458)10xFA mutant and no interaction between FG-coated beads and 3xGFP could be detected (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is directly observed from pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: No interaction between FG-coated beads and 3xGFP could be detected.
source: This interaction was highly specific since ScKap95 did not bind to the Nup116(348–458)10xFA mutant and no interaction between FG-coated beads and 3xGFP could be detected (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is directly observed from pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: ScKap95 was efficiently eluted with 1M NaCl from all the FG-coated beads.
source: Of note, ScKap95 was efficiently eluted with 1M NaCl from all the FG-coated beads consistent with the relatively weak interaction between ScKap95 and FG-repeat regions (Pyhtila and Rexach, 2003) (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed from pulldown assay data and consistent with cited work.

claim: Both MtNup188 and MtNup192 were strongly enriched on all wild-type FG-repeat regions.
source: Intriguingly, both MtNup188 and MtNup192 were strongly enriched on all wild-type FG-repeat regions and did not show significant binding to the Nup116(348–458)10xFA variant.
evidence: This is directly observed from pulldown assay data.

claim: Both MtNup188 and MtNup192 did not show significant binding to the Nup116(348–458)10xFA variant.
source: Intriguingly, both MtNup188 and MtNup192 were strongly enriched on all wild-type FG-repeat regions and did not show significant binding to the Nup116(348–458)10xFA variant.
evidence: This is directly observed from pulldown assay data.

claim: MtNup188 was relatively inefficiently eluted with 1M NaCl from Nup100(1–310) and Nup100(1–610).
source: The only notable deviation from the FG-binding pattern was observed with MtNup188, which was relatively inefficiently eluted with 1M NaCl from Nup100(1–310) and Nup100(1–610), suggesting that MtNup188 either interacts with these FG-repeat regions more tightly than ScKap95 or that these interactions are more hydrophobic in nature (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed from pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Neither MtNup188 nor MtNup192 can form a stable complex with RanGTP.
source: Consistent with this, we were unable to detect binding between RanGTP and either MtNup188 or MtNup192 by gel filtration analysis (Figure 4D) whereas the NTR ScKap95 bound robustly to RanGTP (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly observed from gel filtration binding assays shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: ScKap95 bound robustly to RanGTP.
source: Consistent with this, we were unable to detect binding between RanGTP and either MtNup188 or MtNup192 by gel filtration analysis (Figure 4D) whereas the NTR ScKap95 bound robustly to RanGTP (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly observed from gel filtration binding assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: YFP-importin-β efficiently translocated into nuclei independent of the presence of a nuclear transport mixture.
source: As expected, YFP-importin-β efficiently translocated into nuclei independent of the presence of a nuclear transport mixture (Xenopus cytosol plus energy regeneration system).
evidence: This is directly observed from nuclear translocation assays.

claim: No significant nuclear translocation of 85 kDa 3xGFP was observed in any of the tested conditions.
source: At the same time no significant nuclear translocation of 85 kDa 3xGFP was observed in any of the tested conditions, consistent with the approximately 40–60 kDa diffusion permeability cutoff of intact NPCs (Figure 5A,B) (Mohr et al., 2009).
evidence: This is directly observed from nuclear translocation assays shown in Figure 5 and consistent with cited work.

claim: Both YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 accumulated in intact nuclei even in the absence of a nuclear transport mixture.
source: Strikingly, both YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 mimicked the behavior of YFP-HsImportin-β and accumulated in intact nuclei even in the absence of a nuclear transport mixture.
evidence: This is directly observed from nuclear translocation assays.

claim: Nuclear uptake of YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 was completely blocked in the presence of WGA.
source: Nuclear uptake was completely blocked in the presence of WGA, a broad inhibitor of NPC-mediated transport (Finlay et al., 1987; Mohr et al., 2009) (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is directly observed from nuclear translocation assays shown in Figure 5 and consistent with cited work.

claim: Translocation of both YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192, and of YFP-HsImportin-β, was strongly inhibited upon addition of unlabeled importin-β.
source: Furthermore, translocation of both nucleoporins, and of YFP-HsImportin-β, was strongly inhibited upon addition of an unlabeled importin-β (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is directly observed from nuclear translocation assays shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The translocation of YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 occurs through NPCs.
source: Together these results demonstrate that the translocation of YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 occurs through NPCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the WGA inhibition and competition experiments.

claim: The sizes of YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 (approximately 220 kDa) are far above the diffusion permeability cutoff of the NPCs.
source: Since the sizes of YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 (∼220 kDa) are far above the diffusion permeability cutoff of the NPCs this efficient nuclear translocation cannot be explained by simple passive diffusion.
evidence: This is based on known molecular weights and established NPC permeability limits.

claim: The efficient nuclear translocation of YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 cannot be explained by simple passive diffusion.
source: Since the sizes of YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 (∼220 kDa) are far above the diffusion permeability cutoff of the NPCs this efficient nuclear translocation cannot be explained by simple passive diffusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the size of the proteins and the NPC permeability cutoff.

claim: Both YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 translocated slower than YFP-HsImportin-β.
source: While both nucleoporins translocated slower than YFP-HsImportin-β, their translocation rates exceeded the values of 3xGFP by at least 30-fold indicating that both proteins indeed cross the NPCs in a facilitated manner (Figure 6).
evidence: This is directly observed from kinetic measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: The translocation rates of YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 exceeded the values of 3xGFP by at least 30-fold.
source: While both nucleoporins translocated slower than YFP-HsImportin-β, their translocation rates exceeded the values of 3xGFP by at least 30-fold indicating that both proteins indeed cross the NPCs in a facilitated manner (Figure 6).
evidence: This is directly observed from kinetic measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: Both YFP-MtNup188 and YFP-MtNup192 cross the NPCs in a facilitated manner.
source: While both nucleoporins translocated slower than YFP-HsImportin-β, their translocation rates exceeded the values of 3xGFP by at least 30-fold indicating that both proteins indeed cross the NPCs in a facilitated manner (Figure 6).
evidence: This is inferred from the translocation rate measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: Pre-treatment with RanGTP increased the YFP-MtNup188 translocation rate.
source: While we saw an increase in the YFP-MtNup188 translocation rate, no effect on YFP-MtNup192 was observed.
evidence: This is directly observed from kinetic measurements with Ran pre-wash.

claim: Pre-treatment with RanGTP had no effect on YFP-MtNup192 translocation rate.
source: While we saw an increase in the YFP-MtNup188 translocation rate, no effect on YFP-MtNup192 was observed.
evidence: This is directly observed from kinetic measurements with Ran pre-wash.

claim: After RanGTP pre-treatment, the translocation kinetics of MtNup188 and MtNup192 were approximately equal, but still about fourfold below the values for YFP-HsImportin-β.
source: Under these conditions the translocation kinetics of MtNup188 and MtNup192 were approximately equal, but still about fourfold below the values for YFP-HsImportin-β (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed from kinetic measurements shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The slower nuclear translocation rates of MtNup188 and MtNup192 are intrinsic properties of these two proteins.
source: This suggests that the slower nuclear translocation rates of MtNup188 and MtNup192 are intrinsic properties of these two proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the Ran pre-wash experiments.

claim: Both MtNup188 and MtNup192 accumulated within nuclei in the absence of exogenous energy without reaching notable saturation during the time frame of the experiments.
source: Interestingly, both MtNup188 and MtNup192, unlike HsImportin-β accumulated within nuclei in the absence of exogenous energy without reaching notable saturation during the time frame of our experiments (Figure 6).
evidence: This is directly observed from kinetic measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: Both MtNup188 and MtNup192 continued to accumulate in nuclei even after subsequent 10-fold dilution.
source: Furthermore, both proteins continued to accumulate in nuclei even after subsequent 10-fold dilution, suggesting that they have strong intranuclear binding sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly observed from dilution experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: MtNup188 and MtNup192 have strong intranuclear binding sites.
source: Furthermore, both proteins continued to accumulate in nuclei even after subsequent 10-fold dilution, suggesting that they have strong intranuclear binding sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the continued accumulation after dilution shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: MtNup188 and MtNup192 translocate across NPCs by facilitated diffusion without a requirement for other cytosolic factors.
source: In summary, these results demonstrate that MtNup188 and MtNup192 share functional characteristics with NTRs and translocate across NPCs by facilitated diffusion without a requirement for other cytosolic factors.
evidence: This is concluded from the nuclear translocation assay results.

claim: The topology of Nup188 is distinctly different from all other scaffold nups, except for the related paralog Nup192, in that it appears to be inherently flexible.
source: The analysis of the largest universally conserved nucleoporin Nup188, which we present here, fills the last gap in the inventory of architectural nucleoporin structures. We find that the topology of Nup188 is distinctly different from all other scaffold nups, except for the related paralog Nup192, in that it appears to be inherently flexible.
evidence: This is concluded from structural and EM analysis.

claim: The depletion of Nup188 increases the size limit for the transport of inner nuclear membrane proteins.
source: For instance, the depletion of Nup188 was shown to increase the size limit for the transport of inner nuclear membrane proteins, but this was not observed upon removal of Nup205 (the Nup192 homolog in vertebrates) (Theerthagiri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: The removal of Nup205 (the Nup192 homolog in vertebrates) does not increase the size limit for the transport of inner nuclear membrane proteins.
source: For instance, the depletion of Nup188 was shown to increase the size limit for the transport of inner nuclear membrane proteins, but this was not observed upon removal of Nup205 (the Nup192 homolog in vertebrates) (Theerthagiri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Soluble NTRs and scaffold nucleoporins were considered to be functionally and evolutionarily separated groups of proteins.
source: So far, soluble NTRs and scaffold nucleoporins were considered to be functionally and evolutionarily separated groups of proteins that were already present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor each very likely originating from relatively few ancestor proteins through multiple gene duplication events (Mans et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the prevailing view before this study, supported by a cited reference.

claim: All known NTRs bind FG-repeats, typically exhibiting various binding sites dispersed over their surface.
source: All known NTRs bind FG-repeats, typically exhibiting various binding sites dispersed over their surface (Bednenko et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a cited reference.

claim: The combination of shared FG-binding activity, common NPC translocation properties and general structural similarity suggest that Nup188, Nup192 and NTRs might have a common evolutionary origin.
source: Yet, the combination of shared FG-binding activity, common NPC translocation properties combined and general structural similarity make it tempting to speculate that Nup188, Nup192 and NTRs, indeed, might have a common evolutionary origin.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the combined findings.

claim: Once incorporated into NPCs, Nup188 and Nup192 are unlikely to shuttle across the nuclear envelope.
source: Once incorporated into NPCs Nup188 and Nup192 are unlikely to shuttle across the nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is inferred from the known stability of NPC components.

claim: Nup93 in vertebrate NPCs has very low mobility and exceptionally slow protein turnover.
source: The very low mobility of their common binding partner, Nup93 in vertebrate NPCs and an exceptionally slow protein turnover suggest that both proteins are very stable NPC components (Rabut et al., 2004; Savas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Nup188 and Nup192 are very stable NPC components.
source: The very low mobility of their common binding partner, Nup93 in vertebrate NPCs and an exceptionally slow protein turnover suggest that both proteins are very stable NPC components (Rabut et al., 2004; Savas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of their binding partner, supported by cited studies.

claim: The NTR-like activity of Nup188 and Nup192 could be critical for de novo NPC biosynthesis during interphase nuclear growth in higher eukaryotes or in organisms which undergo a closed mitosis.
source: However, the NTR-like activity of Nup188 and Nup192 could be critical for de novo NPC biosynthesis during interphase nuclear growth in higher eukaryotes or in organisms, which undergo a closed mitosis when new NPCs assemble de novo into the intact nuclear envelope (D'Angelo et al., 2006; Dultz and Ellenberg, 2010; Menendez-Benito et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by cited references about NPC assembly.

claim: Interphase NPC assembly seems to rely on steps that occur on both the cytoplasmic and the nucleoplasmic side of the nuclear envelope.
source: Interphase NPC assembly seems to rely on steps that occur on both the cytoplasmic and the nucleoplasmic side of the nuclear envelope and thus nuclear translocation of NPC components through already existing pores might be critical for new NPC assembly in intact nuclei.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NPC assembly.

claim: Nuclear translocation of NPC components through already existing pores might be critical for new NPC assembly in intact nuclei.
source: Interphase NPC assembly seems to rely on steps that occur on both the cytoplasmic and the nucleoplasmic side of the nuclear envelope and thus nuclear translocation of NPC components through already existing pores might be critical for new NPC assembly in intact nuclei.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on NPC assembly requirements.

claim: FG-scaffold interactions could be important for the structural integrity of the NPC by enabling connections between subcomplexes.
source: Another possibility is that FG-scaffold interactions are important for the structural integrity of the NPC by enabling connections between subcomplexes.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Budding yeast scaffold nucleoporins can be biochemically purified together with NTRs from yeast extracts using FG-repeat regions as a bait.
source: Furthermore, budding yeast scaffold nucleoporins can be biochemically purified together with NTRs from yeast extracts using FG-repeat regions as a bait (Allen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: The interactions between FG-repeats and scaffold nups could be part of the glue that holds the NPC scaffold together.
source: Therefore, the interactions between FG-repeats and scaffold nups could possibly be part of the glue that holds the NPC scaffold together.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: The FG-binding properties of Nup188 and Nup192 might play a role in the correct establishment of the NPC selectivity barrier by organizing the FG meshwork within the NPC channel.
source: Finally, the FG-binding properties that we have discovered here might also play a role in the correct establishment of the NPC selectivity barrier for soluble or transmembrane cargos by organizing the FG meshwork within the NPC channel.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: FG domain interactions with scaffold Nups could connect FG-repeat regions to the wall of the NPC.
source: FG domain interactions with scaffold Nups could connect FG-repeat regions to the wall of the NPC questioning models in which FG-repeats function exclusively within the central channel of the NPC to mediate nuclear transport.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis that questions existing models.
